chunks: "TTL is transistor-transistor logic, built from bipolar transistors: a multi-emitter input transistor and a totem-pole output with an NPN pulling up and an NPN pulling down.
CMOS is built from complementary PMOS and NMOS transistors. The differences fall out of that.
Power: TTL draws current all the time, a couple of milliwatts per gate for 74LS, while CMOS draws almost nothing static and only pays CV to the 2f when it switches.
Inputs: a TTL input has to source current out of the pin when it's low, up to 1. 6 milliamps for standard TTL, and floats high if left open.
A CMOS input is just a gate capacitor, basically zero DC current, but it must never be left floating. Logic levels are the big practical one.
TTL runs at 5 volts with fixed thresholds: inputs see anything above 2. 0 volts as high and below 0. 8 volts as low, and outputs only guarantee 2.
4 volts high, because the totem pole loses a couple of junction drops.
CMOS outputs swing rail to rail and the input thresholds scale with supply, roughly 70% and 30% of V DD for 74HC. So CMOS has much bigger noise margins, but a TTL output's 2.
4 volts doesn't meet a 5 volts 74HC input's 3. 15–3. 5 volts V IH . That's why 74HCT exists: CMOS internals with TTL-compatible input thresholds.
For anything new I'd use CMOS; modern CMOS is faster and lower power. TTL mostly survives as a set of logic-level conventions."
